questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I've always wanted to travel to Australia, so I thought it was a great opportunity to be able to study whilst traveling the country. Also a big part of my decision was that the weather is nice and sunny.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's the best decision. School load is typically less than at home (at least for me and the other exchange students I've talked to). And it is such a great opportunity to be able to experience another culture whilst going to school.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty confusing to be honest. But luckily there is other people who have done it before, and it always works out. It can be a bit frustrating in the beginning though. Mostly the info on school and classes were hard to find.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not anything in particular that I remember. UNSW had a intro meeting and barbecue for exchange students but that was about it. They don't do much to be honest.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They could have made more events so that the exchange students could get to know each other. But it is also a bit hard because I think there's more than 300 exchange students at UNSW - so it is a big group.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
This is a tough one, especially because housing in Sydney is hard and expensive and it is hard to know what is the best solution. If you have a friend/friends you are going with then I would 100% recommend going to Sydney and having booked something temporary. And then when you get here, you can find permanent housing together (rental). 
If you travel alone, then I would definitely recommend finding a student share house (a house where a lot of exchange students live together). This is a great way to get a network and get to know people that are in the same situation as you fast. This will typically be a bit expensive for what you get, but the social part of it makes up for it (to me at least). 
Otherwise, there is also Flatmates Australia where you can find rooms you can rent. 
Only thing I would recommend NOT doing, is getting housing through SCAPE (crazy expensive and not good).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I recommend living off campus. I recommend living by the beaches (Bondi / Coogee), especially in the summer months. Paddington and Surry Hills are also nice, charming areas if you're there when it's not too warm and sunny (and this will be closer to CBD).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I don't think it is possible to live at UNSW when it is only one semester. Also the location is bad.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was just very confusing, and they had a hard time understanding that I was a Masters student since I couldn't send them my Bachelors diploma (I didnn't have it yet because I am a first semester Masters student). Also, theres so many steps back and forth that is just unnecessary, and they don't have an easy system that outlines what courses are available to who.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: So when you get the welcome letter, you have to look into courses. They have three different platforms regarding courses, which makes it very confusing. You have to apply to be approved by UNSW to enroll into courses. It is hard to figure out what courses are available and being offered in my term. When you get approved it doesn't mean that you have been enrolled, it just means that you have met the prerequisites. This is quite annoying because I also had to get approval from Copenhagen University and I didn't know if I'd end up being able to take the course. To make things even more confusing, because I am a law student, I didn't get to pick from my approved courses. UNSW sentt out a list to law exchange students of the courses that were available for us to take - so none of the ones I had looked into beforehand ended up being the courses I got. From the list that were sent to me I had to prioritse between courses, and then they'd enroll us accordingly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They have an E-mail, and I think they are alright at replying. Sometimes it can be a couple of days. They don't have a phone number.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: not at all. But I ended up being happy with 3/4 of my courses, so it worked out okay.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Know that it is frustrating, confusing and that there's so many unnecessary steps - but everything will work out. I know of many that wasn't enrolled in enough courses when they got here. It is easy to make an appointment with school counseling when you're here. Also the first week of the semester is always drop in/drop out week.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's fairly easy. The workload is just very different than in Denmark, because they have several elements that make up the grade.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took easier classes on purpose and made sure to take courses that didn't have any sit-in exams, so that I had more time to travel. So the classes weren't too challenging. Generally, I think the level is pretty low.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It depends on the course. Some courses are very much class room teaching, and then other courses are more lectures.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Winter Term (WT): Australian Legal System In A Comparative Perspective. 

Third Term (T3): 1) International Relations and Sport, 2) Legal Project Management, 3) Introduction to Chinese Regulation of International Business.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Australian Legal System In A Comparative Perspective - Talks about the Australian legal system throughout time and the professor is very interested in other countries' systems. Class full of exchange students. 
International Relations and Sport - it has nothing to do with law. It is a run-through of  historical events where sports have been used as a diplomatic/political arena.. 
Legal Project Management - VERY enthusiastic professor and very practical oriented class. I found it very interesting.

I've spent way more money on travelling than I thought I would. But there's so much to see and visit when you're here so it is very much worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
more expensive: groceries. 
Less exenspise: eating out and coffee (!!)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't try them out. I know that there is a lot of clubs.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot, but I didn't look into it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Didn't try any.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Around Sydney: Blue Mountains, Coastal walks (Coogee-Bondi, Spit-Manly, Coogee-Maroubra), ferry to Manly, explore surry hills, paddington and newtown (vintage shopping is great here). 

Outside of Sydney: Vantrip on the West coast is amazing. So crazy landscape and wild life (important to time it with weather though!). 
Noosa, Byron Bay and Whitsundays on the East Coast are also magical places.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: no - maybe go to some social run clubs. From my experience they keep to themselves and they don't really see much point on socialising with exchane students who will leave soon.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Can't think of any.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Social, active life style.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: To remember that it is a Trimester Uni (at least until 2028, where I think they go back to two Semesters). UNSW start date is much later than all of the other Sydney Uni's. This is quite annoying since many of the exchange students in Sydney had been here for a month when I arrived. This made it a bit harder to find people I connected with, because many had already found their friend groups by the time I arrived. So I recommend coming earlier.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new amazing people, living in Sydney (amazing city that has everything you could dream of), traveling the most beautiful country.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: In the beginning I felt a bit lonely.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
